analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by police and ties federal grants to anti-profiling policies.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban racial profiling by law enforcement gathered 81 cosponsors — every one a Democrat — but never received a hearing or vote, dying in the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement officer to rely on someone's race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, gender, or sexual orientation when deciding whom to stop, search, or question. It would let individuals who were profiled sue, require police agencies to collect and publish stop-and-search data, and require states and cities to adopt anti-profiling policies and complaint procedures as a condition of receiving federal police grants. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again — no hearing, no amendment, no vote — before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are stopped, searched, or questioned by police — particularly Black, Latino, Muslim, and immigrant communities that are disproportionately targeted — would gain a federal right to sue over profiling, plus protections backed by data collection and grant conditions. Every community benefits from published stop data showing whether searches actually find contraband at equal rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People stopped or searched by police

how_it_helps.text: Makes racial profiling illegal for every federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement agent, covering stops, frisks, searches, interviews, and immigration-related investigations [S3].
Allows the Justice Department or any individual injured by profiling to sue for a court order, and makes a statistical pattern of disparate stops prima facie evidence of a violation [S2] [S3].
Requires federal law enforcement agencies to adopt anti-profiling policies, officer training, data collection, and complaint procedures [S2].

Conditions Edward Byrne Memorial and COPS grant funds on state and local agencies maintaining anti-profiling policies, and requires the Attorney General to withhold funds from agencies that do not comply [S2].

Requires annual public reporting of stop and search data, broken down by race, ethnicity, gender, and religion, and funds a demonstration project to measure how often stops actually find drugs or guns — a direct test of whether searches are based on suspicion or on stereotypes [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies bear the costs: new training, data collection systems, complaint procedures, possible loss of federal grant money for noncompliance, and exposure to civil lawsuits. Departments would also face public scrutiny of their stop data.

drawbacks.text: The civil enforcement provision treats statistical disparate impact as prima facie evidence of a violation, which could expose departments to litigation even where individual officers acted on specific, lawful suspicion — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

Compliance requires training, data collection systems, and complaint handling across thousands of agencies, an administrative burden that falls hardest on small departments, though the bill reserves grant funding for small and rural agencies [S3].
Tying federal grant money to compliance gives the Justice Department leverage over local police, which critics view as federal overreach into local policing decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — a federal right not to be stopped or searched because of who you are — is large for the communities most affected and costs taxpayers relatively little, since most of the bill's spending is modest grant money. The costs are real but limited: litigation risk, compliance paperwork, and federal conditions on police grants. The bill is broadly designed, though the disparate-impact evidentiary standard and grant-withholding powers would have invited legal and political challenges.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 10, 2017 by Rep. John Conyers with 57 original cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1] [S3].

It was also referred to two Judiciary subcommittees — Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations, and the Constitution and Civil Justice — on the day of introduction; no further action followed in either [S5].
The bill reached 81 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican support [S4].
After Conyers resigned in December 2017, Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee was made first sponsor in March 2018 for purposes of adding cosponsors; the bill still never advanced [S5].
The House Judiciary Committee never scheduled a markup or hearing, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies are better off: none had to adopt mandatory anti-profiling policies, collect and publish stop data, or face the new civil liability the bill would have created, and federal grants continue without profiling-related conditions. The 115th Congress took no recorded action on racial profiling through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that avoided profiling mandates

for.name: John Conyers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Racial Profiling Act of 2017 and assembled 57 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 81 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

for.name: Sheila Jackson Lee
for.what_they_did: Assumed first sponsorship in March 2018 after the original sponsor's resignation, keeping the bill alive for cosponsor additions.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Bob Goodlatte, R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup in the two years remaining in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 81 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; with Republicans controlling the House and the Judiciary Committee, the bill never got a hearing or a vote.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (state, local, and tribal)
industries.note: Police departments would have had to adopt anti-profiling policies, collect and publish stop data, process complaints, and risk losing Byrne and COPS grant funds for noncompliance, plus face new civil suits. Their institutional interest in avoiding oversight and liability ran against the people the bill would protect from profiling.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (including immigration and customs enforcement)
industries.note: The bill's prohibition and training and complaint requirements explicitly covered enforcement of criminal, immigration, and customs laws, including workplace immigration investigations and border inspections. Federal agencies would have lost the discretion to use national origin and religion in routine enforcement decisions.

The bill authorized grants for anti-profiling training, data-collection technology, and officer feedback systems, creating a funding stream for training and analytics vendors — but only if the bill's mandates created the demand.
